panels.rationale: The image is an axial MRI of the right pectoralis major injury. The caption describes abnormal signal, contour disruption, and retraction along the sternal-head fibers, which is a direct clinical manifestation of pectoralis major rupture.
panels.attribution_text: Magee et al. Complex Intratendinous Pectoralis Major Rupture After Heavy Bench Press.. Cureus 2026. doi:10.7759/cureus.112354. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 1.
panels.figure_caption: Axial magnetic resonance image of the right pectoralis major injury. Axial magnetic resonance image of the right pectoralis major region demonstrating abnormal signal, contour disruption, and retraction along the lateral sternal-head fibers near the anterior axillary fold highlighted by the arrow. The humeral-sided insertional region was interpreted in conjunction with the full MRI series and clinical examination. The preoperative interpretation favored a predominantly myotendinous sternal-head injury, although motion limitation reduced certainty about tendon continuity. Operative exploration later showed intratendinous disruption with limited repairable tendon attached to the retracted muscle.
in_text_mentions: mework, the injury was discussed in terms of acute timing, sternal-head involvement, tear extent, and location along the myotendinous-to-tendinous region [1]. The radiologic impression was a grade 3 myotendinous tear of the sternal head fibers of the right pectoralis major, with a small area of grades 1-2 strain involving the clavicular head fibers. Because motion limited the study, the MRI was interpreted cautiously for tendon continuity and for the amount of tendon remaining attached to the retracted muscle. Representative axial and coronal magnetic resonance images are shown in Figures 1-2.

panels.rationale: Coronal MRI clearly demonstrates retraction and myotendinous disruption of the right pectoralis major consistent with a high-grade rupture, as stated in the figure caption.
panels.attribution_text: Magee et al. Complex Intratendinous Pectoralis Major Rupture After Heavy Bench Press.. Cureus 2026. doi:10.7759/cureus.112354. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 2.
panels.figure_caption: Coronal magnetic resonance image of the right pectoralis major injury. Coronal magnetic resonance image demonstrating edema-like signal and retraction involving the right pectoralis major sternal-head region, highlighted by the arrows. The radiologic impression favored a grade 3 myotendinous tear with a distal tendon stump measuring approximately 30 mm and mild grades 1-2 strains of the clavicular head fibers. Because the study was motion-limited, the MRI was interpreted cautiously for tendon continuity and the amount of tendon remaining on the retracted muscle. Intraoperative findings showed intratendinous disruption requiring extensive mobilization, locking whipstitch fixation through limited tendon and adjacent myotendinous tissue, and cortical button fixation.

panels.rationale: The image is a clinical photograph showing the patient's right anterior chest wall and axillary region. The patient presents with visible loss of muscle contour and loss of anterior axillary fold definition, consistent with clinical presentation of pectoralis major rupture, as documented in the caption.
panels.attribution_text: Stringer et al. Pectoralis Major Rupture in an Active Female.. Journal of the American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons. Global research & reviews 2019. doi:10.5435/jaaosglobal-d-19-00030. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 1.
panels.figure_caption: Clinical picture showing loss of muscle contour of the right anterior chest wall and anterior axillary fold.
in_text_mentions: On examination, there was ecchymosis of the anteromedial right arm. There was loss of pectoralis major muscle contour over the right anterior chest wall, with loss of anterior axillary fold definition (Figure 1). There was tenderness over the site of the humeral insertion of the pectoralis major tendon. Shoulder adduction against resistance was painful. There was no associated rotator cuff muscle weakness, and neurovascular examination of the right upper limb was normal. MRI confirmed rupture of the humeral insertion of the pectoralis major tendon with 40-mm retraction (Figure 2).

panels.figure_caption: Preoperative photo of patient 2 shows asymmetry of the axillary folds; folds are thinned on the left with apparent bunching at the superolateral aspect of the pectoral region.
in_text_mentions: urner presented to our orthopedic outpatient clinic via his general practitioner. He complained of some weakness but primarily of chest wall asymmetry and poor cosmesis to such a degree that he had sought the help of a psychologist 9 months after an injury to his left shoulder sustained while bench pressing. Examination demonstrated bunching of the pectoral muscle, thinning of the anterior axillary fold (Figure 1), and weak shoulder adduction. Because of the detrimental effect the injury was having on the patient's mental health and day-to-day activities, he was offered operative intervention.
